text: Sergey Kobozev (Kostroma, Russian SFSR, Soviet Union; 20 July 1964 – 8 November 1995) was a Russian boxer known for being the first to defeat John Ruiz and as a tough slugger. He was the Cruiserweight Champion of the Soviet Union and, after moving to the United States, became the International Boxing Federation Cruiserweight Champion in July 1994. As an amateur, he held wins over Ali Al-Baluchi and Garry Delaney and competed in several tournaments, including the Army Championships of the Friendly Armies of the Socialist Countries (heavyweight and light heavyweight), the Tammer Tournament (light heavyweight), the President's Cup (heavyweight), the Summer Spartakiad of Peoples of the USSR (light heavyweight), the Giraldo Córdova Cardín Tournament (light heavyweight), the Strandzha Memorial (light heavyweight), the USA–Soviet Union Middle & Heavy Duals (light heavyweight), and the European Championships (light heavyweight). In 1990, Kobozev moved to the United States, living in a fourth-floor apartment on 16th Street in Sheepshead Bay with his live-in companion Yelena Cherskikh and her 7-year-old son, Vitaly. He was managed by Thomas Gallagher and trained by Peter Kahn. He received a shot at the WBC Cruiserweight title vacated by Anaclet Wamba, where he lost via a controversial decision to Marcelo Fabian Dominguez in Paris. He was scheduled to fight Dominguez again on December 13, 1995, for a rematch, which he was training for, and had three major fights coming up. However, on November 8, 1995, Kobozev was reported missing by his girlfriend Lina Cherskikh. He was later found murdered by the Russian mafia after a bar scuffle at Brooklyn's Paradise Club during the weekend of November 3, 1995. His body was buried in a shallow grave and discovered by the FBI in March 1999 in the backyard of Alexander Spitchenko in Livingston, New Jersey. The alleged murderers were Russian mobsters Alexander Nosov and Vasiliy Ermichine, with Natan Gozman, a third defendant, remaining a fugitive until February 2005 when he was arrested in Poland and extradited to New York, where he awaits trial. Prosecutors claimed the mob turned against Kobozev because he worked as a part-time security guard at a Brooklyn restaurant where Nosov was ejected after a fight with a musician. Several days later, the defendants and a third gang member encountered Kobozev at a car repair shop, confronted him about the fight, and Nosov shot him. Still alive, Kobozev was placed in a jeep and driven to the Livingston, N.J., home of a high-ranking mob member, where Ermichine broke his neck after Kobozev requested medical attention. Kobozev's professional record was 22 wins and 1 loss in 23 bouts, and he lost his first career title shot via a split decision on October 24, 1995, for the WBC Cruiserweight title. He disappeared in November 1995, just two weeks after that loss.
